name: Flour / Base
whatItIs: The structural starch -- usually wheat flour, but semolina, ghee-adapted flour blends, or ground nuts in place of some flour all appear across world traditions.
contributes: Structure and crumb; higher-protein flour builds more gluten for chew, while nut flour or semolina shortens the crumb.
interaction: Works directly against fat -- more fat and less gluten development means a shorter, more crumbly result.

name: Fat
whatItIs: Butter, ghee, oil, shortening, or lard -- the ingredient most responsible for a cookie's richness and spread.
contributes: Tenderness, richness, and (depending on temperature when mixed) how much a cookie spreads during baking.
interaction: Melted or very soft fat spreads more during baking than cold fat cut into flour, which is the core lever behind crisp vs. cakey results.

name: Sugar
whatItIs: Granulated, brown, or powdered sugar, or a syrup like golden syrup or dulce de leche used as a sweetener.
contributes: Sweetness, but also structure -- brown sugar's moisture adds chew, while granulated sugar's crystals promote spread and crisp edges.
interaction: Sugar type changes texture as much as flavor -- swapping brown for white sugar in the same recipe measurably changes chewiness.

name: Egg / Binder
whatItIs: Whole egg, egg yolk, whipped egg white, or (in eggless traditions) a liquid-and-leavener substitute that performs the same binding role.
contributes: Moisture, richness, and structure -- whipped egg white specifically can act as the only leavener in a recipe.
interaction: In eggless traditions like Anzac biscuits, the binder and the leavener are often the same step, not two separate ingredients.

name: Leavening
whatItIs: What makes a cookie rise or set with air -- baking soda, baking powder, cream of tartar, whipped egg whites, or nothing at all.
contributes: Spread, lift, and crumb openness; many short, crumbly cookies (shortbread, sablé, polvorón) use no chemical leavener at all.
interaction: Absence of leavening is itself a deliberate choice in several traditions, not an omission -- it's what keeps a dough short and dense rather than a flaw.

name: Flavor
whatItIs: The aromatic core beyond sweetness -- vanilla, cardamom, cinnamon, citrus zest, or a spirit like orange blossom water.
contributes: The identity that distinguishes otherwise structurally similar cookies from each other.
interaction: Flavor choices often signal regional identity directly -- cardamom reads as South Asian, orange blossom water as Levantine, without any other ingredient changing.

name: Mix-ins
whatItIs: Discrete pieces folded through the dough rather than blended in -- chocolate, nuts, oats, or coconut.
contributes: Texture contrast and a secondary flavor that stays distinct from the base dough rather than merging into it.
interaction: Mix-in ratio directly affects spread and structure, not just flavor -- a heavily mixed-in dough often bakes up denser.

name: Filling
whatItIs: A separate component sandwiched or pressed inside the cookie rather than mixed into the dough -- jam, dulce de leche, or a date-and-nut paste.
contributes: The focal point in sandwich and filled cookies, where the surrounding dough is deliberately built to be a supporting texture rather than the star.
interaction: Filled-cookie doughs (Linzer, alfajor, ma'amoul) are almost always more restrained in sweetness than drop-cookie doughs, since the filling supplies most of the sugar.

name: Finish
whatItIs: What happens to a cookie after baking -- a sugar dusting, a chocolate dip, a syrup soak, or nothing at all.
contributes: Visual identity and a final texture or flavor layer distinct from the baked dough underneath.
interaction: Some finishes (cinnamon-sugar on a snickerdoodle) are applied before baking and become part of the crust; others (powdered sugar on ma'amoul) are strictly a post-bake step.
